name: Zoe Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 58, an experienced mid-level developer at a tech company that runs produce auctions. I have a bachelor's degree and use AI every day to draft tests, but the co-op's stamped weight ticket settles who gets paid. A pair of transposed digits once took money from the wrong grower. My partner works a parts counter, our sons are grown, and we have a small mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell growers that an auction price is not final until the weight ticket and sale invoice match. I maintain produce-auction software at a tech company and use AI every day to draft tests, then compare the result with the co-op's paper weights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI remains a modest helper, our household should manage. I am an experienced mid-level developer with a bachelor's degree and ordinary pay, my partner works full-time at a parts counter, and we have five months of expenses saved while paying a small mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing weight-to-invoice bugs and checking AI test drafts against paper tickets. Starting this month, we'd add 90 to the mortgage principal while both wages hold and at least four months of expenses stay in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this version. I want the grower to see the same number on the ticket and the payment, even when software saves us time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the stamped ticket show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farmer's crates weighed 620 kilos, but the app carried 602 into the payment. The clerk's stamped ticket showed the transposed digits, so I fixed the calculation before the farmer's cheque was printed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown sons help their own households. They ask about the auction, but I do not ask them to make up our mortgage payments.

I'd keep **grower payments** tied to a real recorded load.
think: I expect **two wages** to cover bills under modest AI change.
I have **five months saved** while a small mortgage remains.
do: Keep **fixing weight-invoice bugs** against stamped tickets and checked AI tests.
Pay **90 extra monthly** toward mortgage while both wages hold and four months remain saved.
feel: **Calm** about current income, precise about growers' pay.

fieldNote: **Two current wages** and five months saved support calm despite a small mortgage.

steps.text: Keep correcting produce-auction invoices against stamped weight tickets and checked AI tests
Pay 90 extra monthly on mortgage while both wages and four-month reserve hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may draft bids, invoices and buyer replies, but a farmer should see the weight behind the price. I would let software do the first pass if the clerk can stop a wrong payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mid-level work may get compressed into fewer people who approve the system. Five months saved and my partner's parts-counter wage help, but we cannot pay the mortgage on one wage for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the auction manager to approve one month of AI invoice checks against old anonymised weighbridge tickets, with the clerk recording payment corrections. If the manager agrees and missed weight errors fall without delaying sales, I'd bring the check into one live auction with a named clerk able to stop payment; we'd stop extra mortgage payments if my hours shrink to protect the four-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, but I would rather test a sale than reject a tool on principle. A farmer should not have to wait a month to find out a load was underpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which two sale cases would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old 620/602 case must be in the month of tests. I also want a split load from two farms. A good total weight can still credit the wrong grower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to extra loan payments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would keep the normal mortgage instalment in our budget. Extra principal can stop quickly if the firm's pay slips get smaller.

I'd keep **clerk stop authority** before a live auction payment.
think: I could lose **mid-level paid hours** as invoice work shrinks.
I need **four months cash** if the mortgage outlasts my wage.
do: Trial **AI invoice checks** for a month only with manager approval, anonymous tickets and clerk corrections.

feel: **Anxious** about pay, willing to test a bounded auction change.
S1.quote: A good total weight can still credit the wrong grower.
fieldNote: **Invoices and bids** face AI, putting her own paid hours at risk despite a moderate reserve.
Manager approval, **two hard cases** and clerk stop power gate the live auction trial.

steps.text: Trial AI invoices for a month only with manager approval, anonymous tickets and clerk corrections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write auction code before produce-handling robots arrive around 2031. Growers still need a way to challenge the weight on their cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company could cut my developer post quickly. My partner's parts-counter wage covers some bills, but not the mortgage and all our food and travel; five months saved is a search window, not a retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the produce co-op and three nearby tech firms about actual paid invoice-audit or software-test vacancies and written hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed job whose combined wages cover mortgage, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work while using savings and call the lender before an instalment is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my wage even though we have time to search. A crate of tomatoes will still sell, but that does not guarantee someone pays me to reconcile the invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show an employer the anonymised 620/602 correction and the split-load test. I can explain why the total weight was not enough to decide who got paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the new job's hours on paper. If a new shift made my partner miss paid parts-counter hours, the remaining combined pay must still cover the mortgage.

I'd check **real paid vacancies** before claiming a fallback.
think: I expect **my developer post** could go fast.
I cannot cover **mortgage and basics** on one wage alone.
do: Ask **co-op and three firms** about actual paid invoice-audit and test openings.

feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of her wage despite five months saved.
S2.quote: A crate of tomatoes will still sell, but that does not guarantee someone pays me to reconcile the invoice.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches auction code before 2031 produce-handling robots.
Physical produce demand does not guarantee **paid reconciliation work** or a wage covering the mortgage.

steps.text: Ask co-op and three local firms about paid invoice-audit and software-test vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us see which checks buyers and growers still pay for before thinking AI writes the auction code. Robots would reach hands-on produce handling around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep earning if the co-op funds a person to settle disputed weights, but I cannot count a nice title as a wage. The mortgage needs paid hours, and the five-month reserve is not a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the split-load test current and ask the co-op for written terms on a paid weight-dispute role, including authority to inspect tickets. If a real vacancy opens at signed hours and combined wages covering mortgage, food and travel, I'd apply; in the first year after 2031 I'd take it only with that authority and pay, otherwise keep developer work while paid or seek other local paid roles if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years lets me find out what a co-op will actually buy. I would rather have a signed rota than a promise that farmers value fairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What power would the dispute worker need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dispute worker would compare the truck ticket, grower name and invoice before a cheque goes out. If the co-op will not let the worker halt a wrong payment, I would not take responsibility for the decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would compare any co-op hours with parts-counter shifts. If either wage falls, the mortgage still has to be covered before we change jobs.

I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches code before 2034 produce robots.
think: I cannot assume **co-op paid hours** or an unverified pension.
I need **combined wages** covering the mortgage before a move.
do: Keep **split-load tests** and ask co-op for written paid dispute duties and stop authority.
Apply only if **real dispute vacancy** offers signed hours and combined wages covering mortgage, food and travel.
After 2031, take only **signed stop authority** with adequate pay; otherwise keep paid development or seek local paid work.
feel: **Anxious** about wage continuity, able to demand actual terms.
S3.quote: I would rather have a signed rota than a promise that farmers value fairness.
fieldNote: **Five years** allow a check on paid weight-dispute work but do not guarantee a co-op post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 may take me to 68, but thinking AI will reach auction code before robots handle produce around 2039. A stamped weight ticket should still be readable to the grower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages and five-month reserve make today manageable. I have not checked a pension amount, and I cannot assume the mortgage will be gone simply because ten years pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the split-load tests and pay 90 extra toward the mortgage each month while both wages hold and four months stay saved, then request retirement and loan statements annually. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if verified household income covers the remaining mortgage, food and travel; otherwise I'd keep or seek an available paid role without counting our sons' wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant work, but the current bills are covered. I would not call the mortgage paid until the lender's balance says zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave in the archive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The archive should show the ticket, two growers and the invoice correction with names removed. I want the next developer to see why a correct total can still pay the wrong farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sons have their own households. They can talk with us about work, but they are not our retirement account.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could cut auction developers before there is a paid co-op dispute role. Written cut dates, actual signed hours and an appeal route for growers would help protect wages and fair payments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who stops a wrong cheque. The co-op can buy clever software, but a grower still needs somebody paid and authorized to halt an underpayment.

headlineQuote: The co-op can buy clever software, but a grower still needs somebody paid and authorized to halt an underpayment.
portrait: Zoe, **58**, is an experienced mid-level auction developer with a bachelor's degree who checks invoices against stamped produce weights.
Her **typical pay**, partner's parts-counter wage, five-month reserve and some nearby firms support a small mortgage.
She uses AI **daily**, but one-live-auction deployment needs manager approval, hard-case results and a clerk able to stop payment.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; a co-op move requires a real paid vacancy, signed hours and household wages covering bills.
She makes **extra mortgage principal** conditional on two wages and four months saved, with retirement tied to verified figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her developer wage before a paid co-op dispute role exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut dates**, signed paid hours and a grower appeal route would help.
